clips.title: How to Review a Pull Request Like a Senior Developer
clips.why: An experienced reviewer explains where review starts: with the title, the description and the linked issue, before any code. That is the reader our PR body is written for.
look: Notice how much he decides from the description alone, before he opens a single file.
Think about what happens to that trust when one sentence in the description turns out to be false.
The linked issue gives the why. In our body, the Why heading and the References link do that job.
clips.after: A reviewer reads RH-1234's description in the same order, which is why every claim in it must already be checked by the time they get there.

clips.title: What is a Pull Request, and How Do I Write Great Pull Requests?
clips.why: The same speaker, now as the author: pictures, recordings and GitHub's formatting help a reviewer see a change instead of imagining it.
look: Watch for when a recording helps more than words. Our QA plan decides that per check.
Formatting helps a reader scan. Our fixed headings and the folded details block are the same idea.
Ask of each example: is this proof, or decoration? We only attach proof the plan asked for.
clips.after: Nova's videos are proof for one check each, linked from the checks table, recorded on seed data, and never pictures of code or logs.

clips.title: LLM Chronicles #6.7: Faithfulness Checks for RAG pipelines (gpt4o-mini, Llama-index, RAGAS, Azure)
clips.why: A model used as a judge checks whether an answer is supported by its source text. Swap "answer" for "PR description" and "source" for "diff and evidence", and this is our PR judge.
look: The judge gets the answer and the source side by side, and nothing about how the answer was produced.
An answer can sound fluent and still not be supported. Fluency is not proof, in a chatbot or in a PR.
Think about what shape a verdict needs so that code, not a person, can act on it: our answer is a ready flag and a list of items.
clips.after: Our judge does the same check sentence by sentence and returns not_in_diff or no_proof with a suggested rewrite, so Nova fixes the words before a person reads them.

practice.q: Which part of RH-1234's PR body is the model allowed to write?

options.text: The result column of the checks table
options.why: Results come from the QA results file. If the model typed them, a hopeful pass could appear for a check that failed.
What changes, Why and Where to look first are the model's three pieces of prose. Every fact around them is copied by code.
The harness writes it from the run's requester and the people file. A wrong login here would break the rule that the requester never approves.

practice.q: The description says "Handles the loading state too, so the card never flashes." The diff has no loading state, and the receipt lists the flash as left open. Which problem word does the PR judge use?

options.why: The sentence is short. Its problem is that it is not true.
The sentence is very clear. A reviewer would understand it and believe it, which is the danger.
The claim describes code that does not exist in the change. The judge asks for a rewrite that says the flash is still open with the requester.

practice.q: RH-1234's draft has everything clean except one required check, Frontend Unit Tests, which is red. The same check is red on main too. What does Nova do?

options.text: Link main's failing run in the PR as proof and flag the PR for a person
options.why: No change on this branch can make a check green that main itself fails. A person decides, and the link shows the failure is not Nova's.

options.text: Keep pushing small fixes until the check turns green
options.why: The failure is on main, so no fix on the branch can help. Nova would loop and spend money for nothing.

options.text: Re-run the CI workflow until it passes
options.why: Nova never re-runs or starts a CI workflow; each push runs CI by itself. And a red main stays red however often it runs.

practice.q: In render.mjs, the lines() helper makes sure a heading is never left empty. Fill in what it returns for an empty list.
practice.hint: A list item that says there is nothing to list.
practice.why: An empty heading looks like something was forgotten. "- None." says clearly that nothing was skipped, and the shape check can still see the heading.

practice.q: Put the last steps of RH-1234's run in order, from the evidence pack to the first ping.
items: render() writes the body from the evidence pack and the model's three pieces of prose
The PR judge flags two sentences, and Nova rewrites them until the judge accepts the description
Nova opens PR #2512 as a draft through the broker
Byte reviews the draft, and Nova fixes or answers each important finding
The ready gate reads the checks, the QA results, both judges and the open findings, and marks the PR ready
The frontend reviewers are asked for a review and you, the requester, get one Slack message
practice.why: The words are checked before the PR exists, the code is reviewed while it is a draft, and people hear about it only once everything is clean.

practice.q: Before trusting the PR judge, you run it on 10 PRs that people wrote and 10 Nova drafts with planted false claims. It catches all 10 planted claims, and it also flags 9 of the 10 human PRs. Is it ready?

options.text: Yes, because it caught every planted claim
options.why: Catching everything is easy if you flag everything. A judge that complains about almost every PR teaches people and Nova to ignore it.

options.text: No, because it flags most clear, true descriptions too, so its flags mean little
options.why: It must catch the planted claims without flagging most of the human PRs. Here its prompt needs work, for example the line that a clear, true description with nothing to flag is a good result.

options.text: No, because 20 PRs are too few to measure anything
options.why: Twenty is small, but nine false flags out of ten is not luck. The result is clear enough to act on.
